docs.title: Analysis and Reports
docs.text: 中文

docs.title: Report layers
docs.text:
A useful review combines four kinds of evidence:

  1. Eligibility: ELF/symbol range, relocations and detour plan.
  2. Semantic: lifted IR plus original/protected behavior.
  3. Transformation: profile, block ownership, bridges and encrypted payload metadata.
  4. Quality/cost: byte exposure, diversity, size and runtime ratios.

No one metric establishes security. In particular, high entropy may merely indicate compression/encryption, and whole-file similarity is dominated by unprotected code.

docs.title: Built-in commands
docs.text:
./build/myvmp inspect-elf INPUT SYMBOL
./build/myvmp --log-dir DIR protect-dry-run INPUT SYMBOL SEED
./build/myvmp lift-elf-symbol INPUT SYMBOL
./build/myvmp profile-manifest SEED
./build/myvmp quality-report --json BEFORE AFTER

protect sidecars are JSON and include architecture, VM mode, codecs, profiles, physical blocks, profile owner IDs, successors and bridges. protect-many also produces an aggregate batch manifest.

For attacker-oriented structural observations, use scripts/vm_attacker_metrics.py:

python3 scripts/vm_attacker_metrics.py build/protected.elf --output build/attacker.json
python3 scripts/vm_attacker_metrics.py build/a.elf.myvmp.json build/b.elf.myvmp.json
python3 scripts/vm_attacker_metrics.py build/protected.elf --trace build/block-trace.json

The report covers visible profile fingerprints, manifest CFG/owner/bridge structure, implementation-known operand-format reuse, and optional observed block-trace shape. A trace is a JSON block-ID list or {"block_ids": [...]}. Sidecar graph values measure disclosed metadata; this particular sidecar-oriented tool marks an ELF without a sidecar opaque. That status is a tool limitation, not a claim that the runtime format conceals its structure. These values are structural proxies, not recovered semantics or measured devirtualization effort.

For an attacker-side runtime bytecode oracle, use scripts/reference_devirtualizer.py:

python3 scripts/reference_devirtualizer.py build/protected.elf \
  --payload-file-offset 0x123000 --output build/reference-analysis.json
# To ignore an adjacent sidecar, supply the architecture and runtime code size:
python3 scripts/reference_devirtualizer.py build/protected.elf \
  --no-sidecar --architecture aarch64 --runtime-code-size 10024 \
  --payload-file-offset 0x123000 --output build/runtime-only-analysis.json

The file offset is the payload_offset printed by protect; the runtime code size must match the build being examined (10024 is an example, not a format constant). The tool reads native runtime headers for AArch64, ARM32 and RV64, reverses bytecode whitening and operand-window encoding, and recovers physical blocks, owner indices, logical VM opcodes, operand bytes and explicit static branch targets without a sidecar. It derives additional fallthrough edges from instruction boundaries. AArch64 single-VM opcode mapping uses the patched native dispatcher and the checked-out source's comparison order; the other modes use runtime translation tables. With a sidecar, it compares recovered blocks, owners and CFG edges against published metadata. The v3 report keeps VM instruction/CFG recovery separate from source-level semantic IR recovery, which remains zero; dynamic VM-return edges and handler effects are not inferred. These exposed fields should not be interpreted as evidence of semantic protection. Run make reference-devirtualizer-test with all three cross toolchains to check real protected ELF fixtures, including AArch64 single/sibling mode, truncation and malformed size/target/owner data. Consumers should check schema: payload_file_offset is the runtime start and encrypted_bytecode_file_offset is the encrypted VM region (v1 used the former name for the encrypted region).

The current integration fixtures produce these exact sidecar comparisons (sibling mode, seeds 12345/67890):

Protected fixture Runtime blocks Boundary/owner matches VM instructions CFG edge matches AArch64 branch operations 5 5/5 27 6/6 ARM32 VM probe 5 5/5 37 6/6 RV64 integer operations 3 3/3 29 2/2

The same instructions and edges are recovered when each sidecar is ignored. These counts come from the stated fixtures/seeds, not an architecture-wide coverage claim.

The JSON emitted by quality-report --json has the stable top-level identifier "schema": "myvmp-quality-v1". Consumers should check this value before interpreting metrics; additive fields may be introduced in a future schema version. The report exits with status 1 when any requested threshold fails, so CI can treat it as a quality gate.

docs.title: Automated report bundle
docs.text:
The repository includes scripts/generate_analysis_report.py:

python3 scripts/generate_analysis_report.py \
  --tool build/myvmp \
  --input app.arm64 \
  --protected app.protected.arm64 \
  --symbol protected_calculation \
  --output build/reports/app

It writes:

build/reports/app/
  report.md              human-readable summary
  report.json            machine-readable index and metrics
  inspect.txt            ELF/symbol/patch plan
  lift.txt               lifted IR, when a symbol is supplied
  quality.json           before/after byte metrics, when requested
  protected.manifest.json copied sidecar, when present

Use --before-bytes and --after-bytes to compare extracted function/payload byte ranges. Without them the script generates the other evidence but skips quality scanning. Add --whole-elf-quality only when a potentially expensive whole-file comparison is intentional; unchanged application code usually dominates that result.

docs.title: Interpreting quality metrics
docs.text:
Metric Preferred direction Meaning same_position_ratio lower unchanged bytes at the same offset longest_same_position_run lower largest fixed byte island aligned 32/64-bit exposure lower source words found in output literal 32/64-bit exposure lower arbitrary source windows found in output pairwise ciphertext distance higher seed-to-seed payload diversity unique payloads/manifests equal sample count catches fixed profiles or collisions owner balance away from 0 both sibling VMs perform meaningful work bridge count non-zero proves actual cross-profile CFG transitions runtime/size ratio bounded operational cost

Thresholds should be calibrated on representative protected symbols. Whole-file size ratio and similarity are usually misleading for a small protected function.

The FunctionVmIsa API provides an experimental per-function ISA and operand grammar descriptor for specialization studies. It is metadata groundwork only; the current native encoder and runtime still use the shared bytecode operand contract.

docs.title: Recommended release evidence
docs.text: Archive the original hash, protected hash, tool hash/version, full command, seeds through a secret build record, sidecars, report bundle, behavior-test results, target compiler version and runtime/size measurements. Do not publish production seeds if they are treated as build secrets. A seed is diversity input, not a cryptographic root of trust.

docs.title: Android Native Protection — Long-Term Research Plan
docs.text:
中文

Status: research only. This document does not describe a supported target and does not authorize implementation. “Android protection” here means selected functions in NDK shared libraries, not Java/Kotlin/Dex, resources, or an entire APK.

docs.title: Executive conclusion
docs.text:
An Android arm64-v8a proof of concept can reuse much of myVMP, but production Android support is not a small file-format switch. Android native code is ELF, so the AArch64 decoder, IR, bytecode, dynamic profiles, multi-VM model and most runtime semantics are valuable immediately. The difficult work is safe ET_DYN rewriting under Android linker rules, build-pipeline placement, stripped-symbol selection, 4/16 KiB page compatibility, APK/AAB packaging and signing, and validation across API levels and devices.

The recommended long-term objective is therefore an Android NDK-library protection pipeline, beginning with arm64-v8a. It should transform unstripped .so outputs after native linking and before stripping, packaging, alignment and signing. Direct mutation of a signed APK is the wrong primary architecture.

Under the assumptions of one experienced binary-tooling engineer and a controlled sample app, an arm64 proof of concept is likely several engineer-weeks. A production arm64-v8a integration is more plausibly a multi-month effort once compatibility and release gates are included. Broad ABI coverage is substantially larger: armeabi-v7a normally emits Thumb-2, while x86/x86-64 require new backends. These are planning ranges, not schedules.

docs.title: What an Android app actually contains
docs.text:
Android apps commonly combine ART bytecode and native shared libraries. NDK libraries are ELF files placed at lib/<abi>/lib<name>.so inside an APK; supported NDK ABIs currently include armeabi-v7a, arm64-v8a, x86, and x86_64. Android is little-endian. A fat APK may carry several ABI copies, while App Bundles let Google Play generate device-specific APKs. Android ABI documentation

The native library is loaded by System.loadLibrary, Bionic's dynamic linker and the platform namespace policy. JNI methods may be found by exported names, but Android's recommended model is JNI_OnLoad plus RegisterNatives, often with every other symbol hidden by a version script. This makes a release .so a hostile input for name-based function selection unless protection happens before strip or consumes a linker-produced selection manifest. JNI guidance, symbol visibility

Native libraries may remain uncompressed and be loaded directly from the APK rather than extracted. Current Android guidance also requires native dependencies and ELF load segments to work with 16 KiB page-size devices; NDK r28 makes 16 KiB ELF alignment the default. Packaging behavior, 16 KiB page guidance

docs.title: Recommended pipeline
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[C/C++ source] --> B[NDK Clang + lld]
    B --> C[Unstripped ABI-specific .so]
    C --> D[myVMP Android validator and selector]
    D --> E[Protected .so + private manifest]
    E --> F[llvm-strip / symbols archive]
    F --> G[Gradle package or AAB]
    G --> H[zip alignment and signing]
    H --> I[APK / Play delivery]

The transformer belongs before packaging and signing. apksigner explicitly warns that changing an APK after signing invalidates its signature and that zipalign must precede signing. A post-package fallback could unpack an unsigned APK, transform every selected ABI library, rebuild, align and sign it, but it is more fragile and does not map cleanly to Play-generated APKs from an AAB. apksigner documentation, app signing, bundle/command-line build

The preferred integration points are:

  1. a standalone command that accepts one unstripped NDK .so, ABI, symbol/range manifest, minimum SDK and output path;
  2. a stable Gradle-facing wrapper that operates on native build artifacts without making the core library depend on Android Gradle Plugin internals;
  3. optional CMake/ndk-build examples that run after link and before strip/package;
  4. a packaging verifier, not an APK signer: signing keys must remain owned by the existing Android release system.

docs.title: Reuse of the current project
docs.text:
Existing component Reuse outlook Android-specific work AArch64 decoder/lifter and scalar semantics High Expand NDK/Clang corpus and Android call/addressing forms ARM32 A32 frontend Limited NDK emits Thumb-2 by default; forcing ARM mode is only a constrained fallback RV64 frontend Future only Not a current public NDK app ABI; do not expose as Android support yet Common IR, bytecode and operand codec Very high Add Android qualification, limits and manifest fields Dynamic/sibling multi-VM High Validate JNI calls, exceptions, threads and realistic stack budgets Native runtime assembly High for arm64 Android/Bionic ABI audit, BTI/PAC properties and unwinding policy ELF parser and planner Medium-high Android relocations, notes, dynamic tags, RELR/packed forms and strict ET_DYN tests ELF writer/detours Medium Preserve 4/16 KiB PT_LOAD alignment, GNU RELRO and loadability from APK Sidecars and quality reports High Keep detailed manifests outside the shipped APK by default QEMU Linux tests Partial Add emulator/device, adb, logcat, JNI and API-level matrices

The current runtime executes native interpreter code from an executable ELF mapping and keeps mutable bytecode/state in data/stack memory, so it does not inherently require a JIT-style writable-and-executable mapping. That is a useful fit for Android W^X policy, but it must be verified on real Android loaders rather than inferred from Linux QEMU.

docs.title: 1. Define the supported artifact and ABI contract
docs.text:
• Scope v1 to app-owned NDK .so files, initially arm64-v8a and selected scalar functions; explicitly exclude framework/system libraries, DEX and resources.
  • Record minSdk, ABI, NDK/Clang/LLD/AGP versions, page-size mode and JNI registration strategy in a build manifest.
  • Decide whether C++ exceptions/unwind tables, sanitizers, LTO and CFI are rejected first or supported with explicit metadata repair.

docs.title: 2. Make function selection survive release builds
docs.text:
• Protect before strip whenever possible.
  • Support a source/link-time selection file containing stable symbol, section, address range and optional build ID, rather than depending only on .symtab.
  • Preserve JNI_OnLoad, exported JNI entry points and every address referenced by RegisterNatives; verify that detours do not invalidate registration tables.
  • Define behavior for identical code folding, LTO cloning, COMDAT and local/hidden symbols.

docs.title: 3. Harden ELF rewriting for Android ET_DYN
docs.text:
• Build a corpus from multiple NDK releases and API levels.
  • Validate Android/AArch64 and ARM relocation families, GNU/Android RELR or packed relocation metadata, .dynamic, GNU hash, build ID, symbol versions and RELRO.
  • Preserve p_offset ≡ p_vaddr (mod p_align) and both 4 KiB and 16 KiB PT_LOAD alignment.
  • Test PIE load bias, ASLR, direct-from-APK loading, lazy/eager binding and linker namespaces. Android's Bionic notes document platform-specific linker evolution, including RELR compatibility. Bionic linker changes
  • Decide how unwind metadata is handled. The safe first policy is to reject selected functions whose exception/unwind behavior cannot be preserved.

docs.title: 4. Qualify runtime and ABI behavior
docs.text:
• Test JNI ordinary, @FastNative and @CriticalNative entry ABIs separately; the latter changes the native signature and has API-level constraints.
  • Verify thread-local JNIEnv, callbacks into ART, native helpers, signals, stack alignment, alternate thread stack sizes and recursion depth.
  • Audit AArch64 GNU properties and modern control-flow features such as BTI/PAC when emitted by the toolchain; never remove a property merely to make a fixture load.
  • Measure startup, JNI-call latency, memory, APK/AAB size and per-function overhead on physical devices, not only emulators.

docs.title: 5. Integrate packaging without owning secrets
docs.text:
• Produce transformed .so artifacts for Gradle to package through jniLibs or the external native build pipeline. Android supports both CMake/ndk-build integration and prebuilt libraries. Gradle native build integration, NDK CMake toolchain
  • Verify ABI directory placement, compression and ZIP/page alignment.
  • Let Gradle, Play App Signing or the owner's existing release system sign outputs; myVMP must not accept or store production signing keys.
  • Treat detailed protection manifests and seeds as private CI artifacts, not APK assets.

docs.title: 6. Add Android-specific release gates
docs.text:
• Minimal JNI app with deterministic native behavior for each supported ABI.
  • Debug/release, stripped/unstripped, APK/AAB, extracted/direct-load and 4/16 KiB cases.
  • Emulator matrix plus representative physical devices/API levels; compare JNI results, crashes, logcat, load time and memory.
  • readelf/llvm-readobj, zipalign -c, apksigner verify, bundletool alignment checks and installation/upgrade tests.
  • Negative fixtures for stripped selection, unsupported relocations, Thumb input, malformed packages, unwind/CFI conflicts and insufficient detour space.

docs.title: Difficulty by target
docs.text: Milestone Relative difficulty Reason Standalone arm64-v8a .so proof of concept Medium Core ISA and VM exist; Android ET_DYN and packaging validation do not Production arm64-v8a Gradle pipeline High Toolchain/version matrix, symbols, 16 KiB, signing order and device qualification Constrained armeabi-v7a built with -marm Medium-high Existing A32 can help, but compiler corpus and Android ABI still need qualification Normal armeabi-v7a support Very high NDK defaults to Thumb-2 and permits Neon, neither covered by the A32 backend x86/x86_64 Android support Very high Requires new ISA frontends, runtimes and detours Java/Kotlin/Dex obfuscation Separate project Different formats, runtime and threat model; existing native VM is not a shortcut Turnkey APK/AAB multi-ABI product Very high/ongoing Combines every backend with Gradle, Play delivery and long-lived compatibility testing

docs.title: Recommended staged roadmap
docs.text:
1. Feasibility corpus: collect unstripped/stripped arm64-v8a libraries from supported NDK versions; report liftability and layout compatibility without writing files.
  2. Standalone arm64 .so: protect one hidden scalar function selected before strip; load it in a minimal JNI app on emulator and a 16 KiB-capable device image.
  3. Android-safe writer: pass relocation, RELRO, 4/16 KiB, direct-from-APK and malformed input gates; publish an Android-specific manifest schema.
  4. Build integration: add a versioned standalone wrapper and sample Gradle/CMake hook, then verify APK and AAB workflows before signing.
  5. Production qualification: NDK/AGP/API/device matrix, performance budgets, crash diagnostics, reproducibility and upgrade testing.
  6. ABI expansion: choose Thumb-2 or x86-64 based on actual deployment demand; do not claim full Android coverage while only arm64-v8a is protected.

docs.title: Decision gates before implementation
docs.text: Implementation should begin only after the project chooses a minimum Android API level, supported NDK/AGP range, initial ABI, symbol-selection integration and policy for unwind, LTO/CFI and 16 KiB devices. The first deliverable should be a compatibility/liftability report, not an APK rewriting command.

docs.title: Architecture and Protection Pipeline
docs.text: 中文

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
myVMP is a host-side binary transformer. Its unit of protection is a named function in a linked little-endian ELF executable or shared object. It does not parse C/C++, require an LLVM pass, or replace the operating-system loader. The output remains a native ELF and enters an embedded target-ISA interpreter only when protected code is called.

flowchart LR
    A[Linked ELF + symbol] --> B[ELF validation]
    B --> C[ISA decoder/lifter]
    C --> D[Architecture-neutral IR]
    D --> E[CFG and VM bytecode]
    E --> F[Dynamic profile + codecs]
    F --> G[Native VM runtime payload]
    G --> H[ELF layout planner/writer]
    H --> I[New protected ELF + manifests]

Every stage produces a complete object before the next stage publishes anything. A failure leaves the input untouched and prevents a partial final output.

docs.title: ELF model and planning
docs.text:
src/elf reads ELF32/ELF64 metadata into width-neutral segments, sections, symbols and relocations. Table sizes, file ranges and virtual ranges are checked before indexing. Patch planning determines whether a target symbol is file backed, executable, large enough for a detour and free of unsupported in-range relocations.

src/patch owns architecture-specific entry encoders and ELF writers. PC-relative distance calculation is shared and overflow safe. ELF64 AArch64 and RV64 writing shares a target-parameterized layout engine, but detour encodings remain separate. AArch64 can use a direct branch, a position-independent ADRP/ADD/BR far detour, or the supported non-PIE literal fallback. RV64 selects its corresponding near/far sequence. ARM32 uses an A32 direct branch when representable and an eight-byte absolute literal detour for far ET_EXEC placement; overflow and insufficient-entry cases fail closed.

docs.title: ISA frontends
docs.text:
src/arm64, src/riscv64 and src/arm32 decode native instructions and lift their semantics. Frontends know native register roles, widths, PC-relative addressing and instruction-specific side effects, but they do not know ELF injection policy or native runtime layout.

An unknown or unsafe instruction is not emitted as an opaque VM operation. The complete function is rejected. This avoids a protected binary that works only on untested paths.

docs.title: Common IR
docs.text: src/ir represents register operations, flags, memory, control flow, calls, floating point and supported atomic semantics independently of the source ISA. Explicit block and branch structure lets the encoder change physical order without changing logical CFG. Validation rejects invalid registers, targets, widths and programs without valid exits.

docs.title: Bytecode and profiles
docs.text: src/bytecode is the single source of truth for the logical VM ISA, operand widths, physical opcode domains, profile generation and payload encoding. A stable logical operation is mapped to a seed-specific physical representation. All target runtimes consume the same format contract through include/myvmp/runtime/format.hpp and shared profile tables.

docs.title: VM execution models
docs.text: src/vm/vm.cpp is the host semantic interpreter used for fast correctness tests. src/vm/multi_vm.cpp defines sibling ownership, bridge metadata and validation. Host normalization is a test mechanism; protected target binaries decode their current profile dynamically in native runtime code.

docs.title: Native runtimes
docs.text:
runtime/aarch64_vm.S, runtime/riscv64_vm.S and runtime/arm32_vm.S are auditable assembly sources. Generation scripts assemble them with the relevant cross toolchain and produce checked-in byte includes. Normal host builds therefore do not require a cross assembler; make check-*-runtime proves source and generated blobs agree.

The runtime payload contains native dispatcher code, immutable/encrypted profile metadata, physical block metadata and encrypted bytecode. Architectural state is held in a complete VM frame. Native call gates synchronize the state required by the target ABI before calling unvirtualized helpers and restore VM execution afterward.

All three runtimes resolve a seed-specific physical opcode through runtime translation tables and decode an operand window using a position-, opcode- and owner-derived stream. ARM32 sibling mode assigns CFG blocks to either of two tables and changes domains at explicit VM control-flow edges, matching the common multi-VM contract.

docs.title: Protection orchestration
docs.text: src/protect connects validation, lifting, encoding, runtime construction and patching. Architecture-specific protectors return a common result model. Sidecar publication is centralized and validates sibling metadata before indexing it. protect-many stages each function and publishes metadata plus the final ELF transactionally after every function succeeds.

docs.title: Detailed transformation
docs.text:
For a selected symbol, the protector:

  1. Parses the ELF and resolves a unique non-empty symbol range.
  2. Confirms target machine/class, executable file backing and safe patch space.
  3. Classifies relocations and supplies file-backed address reads to the lifter.
  4. Decodes the complete function and lifts it using its real virtual address.
  5. Validates IR and discovers CFG leaders, blocks and explicit successor edges.
  6. Generates one or two seeded VM profiles and lowers IR into physical bytecode blocks.
  7. Applies immediate polymorphism, duplicate opcodes, bounded superoperators, block layout changes, operand encoding and encrypted rolling block payloads.
  8. Builds a target-native runtime containing only the format and state needed to execute the image.
  9. Plans aligned executable placement, repairs affected ELF offsets and segment sizes, and installs a near or far entry detour.
  10. Replaces the remaining original native body with seed-derived trap fill.
  11. Writes the new ELF and a reproducibility/ownership manifest.

docs.title: Runtime control flow
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> EntryDetour
    EntryDetour --> SaveNativeState
    SaveNativeState --> LocatePhysicalBlock
    LocatePhysicalBlock --> SelectOwnerProfile
    SelectOwnerProfile --> DecodeOpcodeAndOperands
    DecodeOpcodeAndOperands --> HandlerVariant
    HandlerVariant --> ReencodeWindow
    ReencodeWindow --> NextDispatch
    NextDispatch --> LocatePhysicalBlock
    HandlerVariant --> NativeCallGate: external call
    NativeCallGate --> NextDispatch
    HandlerVariant --> RestoreNativeState: VM return
    RestoreNativeState --> [*]

The dispatcher derives ownership from the current physical block. It does not select one static global VM for the entire function. Operand bytes are decoded for the current instruction window and re-encoded before the next dispatch boundary.

docs.title: Extending the system
docs.text: A new source ISA should implement decoder/lifter, target runtime builder, trampoline and ELF target traits while reusing IR, bytecode, profiles, sibling model, manifests and quality tooling. A new logical operation requires IR semantics, one declared operand layout, host execution, target handlers and tests. Keeping format knowledge centralized prevents one runtime from silently interpreting a different bytecode dialect.

docs.title: Minimal host environment
docs.text:
• GNU Make
  • C++20 compiler (g++ by default)
  • Python 3
  • standard ELF development headers (elf.h, normally supplied by libc development files)
  • binutils for release stripping and inspection

Ubuntu/Debian example:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install build-essential clang python3 binutils

Build and test:

make -j$(nproc)
make test

Check the embedded release version:

./build/myvmp --version

Override tools conventionally:

make CXX=clang++ STRIP=llvm-strip -j$(nproc)
make BUILD_DIR=build-debug CXXFLAGS='-std=c++20 -O0 -g -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror'

docs.title: Cross toolchains and QEMU
docs.text:
For the complete target test suite on Ubuntu/Debian:

sudo apt-get install \
  gcc-aarch64-linux-gnu binutils-aarch64-linux-gnu \
  gcc-riscv64-linux-gnu binutils-riscv64-linux-gnu \
  gcc-arm-linux-gnueabihf binutils-arm-linux-gnueabihf clang \
  qemu-user

Expected commands include aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc, riscv64-linux-gnu-gcc, arm-linux-gnueabihf-gcc, Clang (used to assemble the ARM32 runtime), their objdump/as companions, and qemu-aarch64, qemu-riscv64, qemu-arm.

Clang may be used for corpus generation when a target sysroot is configured, but runtime blob generation scripts currently expect the GNU cross tools named in the Makefile.

docs.title: Windows with WSL2
docs.text:
Install Ubuntu under WSL2 and clone the repository inside its Linux filesystem rather than a Windows-mounted drive for best I/O performance. Then use the Ubuntu commands above. WSL2 is the preferred Windows workflow because the tool, generated ELF files, cross compilers and QEMU all run in their intended Linux environment.

wsl --install -d Ubuntu-24.04

After Ubuntu starts:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install build-essential clang python3 binutils \
  gcc-aarch64-linux-gnu gcc-riscv64-linux-gnu gcc-arm-linux-gnueabihf \
  binutils-aarch64-linux-gnu binutils-riscv64-linux-gnu binutils-arm-linux-gnueabihf qemu-user
git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_URL myVMP
cd myVMP
make -j$(nproc) test

Native Visual Studio/MinGW compilation is not a supported release path: <elf.h>, shell automation, GNU target tools and QEMU-user behavior would otherwise need separate ports.

docs.title: macOS and cross-platform container
docs.text:
Docker Desktop, Podman or another Linux-container runtime provides the same Ubuntu 24.04 environment on macOS and Windows:

docker build -t myvmp:0.1.0 .
docker run --rm myvmp:0.1.0 build/myvmp --version
docker run --rm myvmp:0.1.0 make release-check

To protect files from the current host directory, mount it separately:

docker run --rm -v "$PWD/samples:/work" myvmp:0.1.0 \
  /workspace/build/myvmp protect /work/app.arm64 target /work/app.protected.arm64 1001

On PowerShell use ${PWD}/samples:/work in the volume argument. Container outputs may be owned by the container user on Linux; use a matching --user when needed. Apple Silicon runs an arm64 Ubuntu container by default; the checked-in target runtime blobs keep the host tool build independent of target architecture.

A native macOS port is intentionally deferred. It would require a maintained ELF type compatibility layer and replacements for Linux/GNU test tooling while still producing Linux ELF output; the container gives a smaller, reproducible support surface today.

docs.title: Runtime blobs
docs.text:
Checked-in native runtime blobs let a normal host build succeed without cross tools. After editing runtime assembly:

make generate-aarch64-runtime
make check-aarch64-runtime
make generate-riscv64-runtime
make check-riscv64-runtime
make generate-arm32-runtime
make check-arm32-runtime

Generated includes must be reviewed together with their assembly source. Do not hand-edit the .inc byte arrays.

docs.title: Sanitizer and static audit build
docs.text:
make BUILD_DIR=build-sanitize \
  CXXFLAGS='-std=c++20 -O1 -g -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer' \
  LDFLAGS='-fsanitize=address,undefined' -j$(nproc)
ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0 UBSAN_OPTIONS=halt_on_error=1 \
  build-sanitize/myvmp_tests

Leak detection may be unavailable under ptrace/managed runners; disabling it does not disable address or undefined-behavior checks.

docs.title: Release and package
docs.text:
make release
make package

make release builds with -O3 -DNDEBUG, strips the host tool and assembles English and Chinese documentation. Release objects use an isolated build/release-build tree, so a prior debug/development build cannot be reused accidentally. make package creates build/dist/myvmp-<version>-linux-<host-arch>-tool.tar.gz with a myvmp-<version>/ root directory.

If the host environment supports static C++ linking:

make release STATIC=1
make package STATIC=1

Version comes from VERSION; myvmp --version, archive name and archive root must agree. Release publication and signing are maintained through the repository hosting platform.

Before publishing, run make reproducible-check package-smoke-test. This compares two isolated release builds with a fixed SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH, normalizes tar ownership/order/ timestamps, and then extracts the package to verify the binary and required documentation.

docs.title: Obfuscation and Multi-VM Design
docs.text: 中文

docs.title: Design objective
docs.text: myVMP aims to remove a stable correspondence between source instructions and protected bytes while preserving deterministic reproduction and bounded runtime cost. Diversity is layered: no single permutation or cipher is treated as sufficient.

docs.title: Dynamic profile
docs.text:
A non-zero seed derives a complete VmProfile. Different seeds affect:

  • logical-to-physical opcode permutation and duplicate semantic opcode selection;
  • rolling payload keys and operand-window codec material;
  • dispatcher comparison-domain constants and native handler variant masks;
  • two- or three-stage immediate reconstruction templates and independent shares;
  • non-entry basic-block order and explicit successor encoding;
  • original-body trap fill and other placement-specific constants.

The profile manifest records enough information to reproduce and diagnose an output. Reproducibility is deliberate: a failing seed can be investigated without making all builds identical.

docs.title: Logical and physical opcodes
docs.text:
The common VM ISA has stable logical operations used by IR and tests. A profile maps them onto physical opcode bytes. High-frequency operations also have duplicate physical encodings selected per occurrence, so learning one physical value does not identify every instance of the same semantics.

The native dispatcher reverses only the mapping needed for the current instruction and selects a seed-derived handler implementation. Unsupported or malformed values enter a fail-closed bad-opcode path.

docs.title: Unified operand codec
docs.text:
Every logical operation declares its operand width centrally. For all operations with operands, the encoder mixes payload key material, physical opcode, physical instruction offset and operand-byte position. The native runtime decodes the current operand window immediately before its handler and re-encodes it before the next dispatch.

Consequences:

  • the same register or immediate has different stored bytes at different positions;
  • adding an opcode with a declared layout automatically enters the codec contract;
  • a plaintext global operand stream is not left beside encrypted opcode bytes;
  • handler decoding remains consistent across the full logical opcode set.

docs.title: Immediate polymorphism
docs.text:
Constants and immediate operations are reconstructed through seed-, block- and instruction-specific equivalent sequences. Examples include XOR shares, modular add/subtract shares and mixed three-stage forms. Branch targets are remapped after expansion using actual physical sizes, not assumed logical positions.

This is bounded polymorphism rather than arbitrary MBA generation: templates are small, fully covered by host semantics and validated under QEMU. It reduces literal exposure without allowing uncontrolled expression growth.

docs.title: CFG-aware blocks
docs.text:
The encoder discovers IR basic-block leaders and assigns stable logical identities. Physical images carry block ranges and explicit successors. Non-entry blocks may be shuffled because conditional fallthrough, jumps and VM-call continuation do not rely on source adjacency.

Encryption evolves per physical block using CFG identity and owning profile. Only boundary information required for execution is stored; derived rolling keys are not serialized as a plaintext table. Identical logical bytes placed in different blocks or owned by different sibling profiles therefore receive different streams.

docs.title: Superoperators and handler variants
docs.text:
Bounded superoperators combine selected adjacent compare/test and branch patterns inside one block. Fusion is forbidden across branch targets, calls, memory-order boundaries or operations whose trapping behavior cannot safely be combined.

Native runtimes contain alternative implementations for common arithmetic, logic, comparison, move, memory, branch and select families. The current profile chooses variant masks. This changes handler bodies and dispatcher paths in addition to changing bytecode.

docs.title: Sibling multi-VM
docs.text:
Sibling mode partitions physical CFG blocks between two independent profiles:

flowchart LR
    A0[VM-A entry block] -->|A bridge B| B1[VM-B block]
    B1 --> B2[VM-B block]
    B1 -->|B bridge A| A3[VM-A block]
    B2 -->|B bridge A| A3

Each block has an owner. Every static cross-owner CFG edge has an explicit VmBridge containing source/destination profile identifiers, continuation and destination blocks, state policy, key epoch, memory-order metadata and a depth bound. The runtime derives the owner on every block transition and switches opcode translation plus handler variants dynamically.

The native runtimes currently share one complete execution frame, so GPRs, FP/SIMD state, SP, flags, VM return state and memory semantics do not pass through a lossy native ABI. The host reference interpreter now additionally models distinct encoded state frames per profile and applies reversible liveness-selected transformations at cross-profile edges. While an internal VM call is active, cross-profile edges transfer complete state so caller registers used after return survive; the host interpreter uses the continuation block's live-ins for the dynamic return edge, which is not a static VmBridge. These state layouts and transforms are not yet consumed by target assembly. CFG loops can cross profiles without recursively nesting interpreter frames. Unknown owners, missing bridges, same-profile bridges, inconsistent partitions and invalid depth metadata are rejected.

This design is intentionally different from unrestricted recursive virtualization. It delivers per-block VM changes without multiplying interpreter stacks or exception/call ABI risk. Selective nested protection remains a possible experiment, not a current claim.

docs.title: What varies at each level?
docs.text: Level Operational variability Build seeds, keys, dispatcher constants, runtime variants, trap fill Function profile(s), CFG partition, physical block order Basic block owner profile, rolling key domain, successor encoding Instruction physical/duplicate opcode, operand window, immediate template Handler entry current mapping entry, decoded operands, selected native variant

docs.title: Quality gates
docs.text:
The project measures, among other things:

  • unique payloads/manifests across seeds;
  • minimum and average pairwise ciphertext distance;
  • same-position byte overlap and longest equal run;
  • aligned word and arbitrary literal-window exposure;
  • output-size and runtime ratios;
  • multi-VM bridge count and ownership balance;
  • complete original/protected behavior under QEMU.

These tests detect regressions such as a fixed opcode map or exposed constants. They do not prove that a skilled analyst cannot recover semantics. See the security model and analysis guide.

docs.title: Experimental attacker and synthesis models
docs.text:
scripts/reference_devirtualizer.py reads AArch64, ARM32 and RV64 runtime headers and reverses bytecode whitening and operand-window encoding to recover physical blocks, owners, VM instructions and static CFG edges directly from protected ELFs. An optional sidecar checks the recovered structure against ground truth. The exposed header key also undoes AArch64's owner-table XOR, so neither that table nor the bytecode encoding should be treated as secret. The oracle does not reconstruct handler effects, source-level semantic IR or dynamic VM-return edges.

Two host-side models are also available. The superoperator miner reports bounded, repeated, side-effect-free scalar opcode sequences confined to a single CFG block; it does not emit bytecode or handlers. The state-representation model provides reversible profile-local GPR, FP, vector, flags, and SP layouts and live-mask transforms. The host sibling interpreter executes this model; native runtime bridges do not consume it yet. Neither model currently changes emitted native protection bytes.

docs.title: AArch64 Advanced SIMD
docs.text:
The AArch64 backend has an explicit fixed-width 128-bit Advanced SIMD subset. It uses a 32-register Vector128 file separate from scalar GPRs, typed 8/16/32/64-bit lanes, nine seed-mapped VM opcode families and the same per-instruction operand codec used by scalar bytecode. Implemented families cover integer add/sub and bitwise operations, signed compare, bit select, immediate logical shifts, EXT, Q load/store, FP32/FP64 vector add/sub/mul/div and zero materialization. Native calls synchronize q0-q7 while preserving the VM-owned vector frame; sibling profiles independently remap all vector opcodes.

Only Q=1 fixed 128-bit forms in the documented subset are accepted. Other NEON forms, AArch64 SVE/SVE2/SME and RV64 Vector remain fail-closed rather than being silently scalarized.

docs.title: CactiVM: Selective Multi-Architecture Binary Virtualization for ELF Functions
docs.text:
中文 · Technical paper draft, 2 October 2026

Author: Yuchen Mu

This is an implementation-grounded research manuscript, not a peer-reviewed paper or a claim of cryptographic security. Measurements below are reproducible fixture results, not a comparison against commercial protectors or a large application corpus.

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: Virtualization-based software protection replaces selected native instructions with a bytecode program executed by an embedded interpreter. Its practical difficulty lies less in choosing a private opcode numbering than in preserving binary interfaces, control flow, memory effects and deployment constraints across real executables. We present CactiVM, a function-selective ELF transformer for AArch64, ARM32/A32 and RV64. It lifts a named function into a common intermediate representation (IR), partitions its control-flow graph (CFG), encodes it with seed-derived VM profiles, embeds a target-native runtime and patches the original entry. Sibling mode assigns physical blocks to two profiles and switches their decoding domain at CFG edges. The implementation includes bounded immediate rewriting, duplicate physical opcodes, selected superoperators, operand-window encoding and architecture-specific native handlers. Correctness is evaluated with host semantic tests and original-versus-protected QEMU runs. A reference attacker tool reverses the shipped runtime format and recovers VM instructions and static CFG edges without the optional manifest. This result demonstrates an important limit: the existing encoding adds diversity but is not a confidentiality boundary. The contribution of this manuscript is an auditable, cross-ISA engineering design and a measurement methodology that reports both protection transformations and attacker-visible structure.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
Function-level protection is useful when an application has a small number of sensitive routines and whole-program virtualization would impose unacceptable size, runtime or compatibility cost. A practical protector must operate after linking, preserve the native calling convention and make no assumption that every instruction family is supported. For ELF, it must also account for symbol ranges, relocations, segment layout, executable placement and detour reach. These requirements are especially visible when extending a single-architecture prototype to three instruction sets.

CactiVM's unit of transformation is a named, file-backed function in a little-endian ELF. The input remains unchanged; the output is another executable or shared object. The protector does not require an LLVM pass or a custom loader. It rejects an unsupported native instruction or unsafe binary range instead of passing that operation through an unmodeled VM instruction. This scope is deliberate: the system protects selected functions, not all code in an ELF, and it does not claim to protect data once a capable analyst observes plaintext execution state.

The engineering contributions are:

  1. A common IR and bytecode contract shared by three target-specific decoders, ELF patchers and native runtimes.
  2. A layered, seed-derived encoding in which build, block and instruction choices can differ, including sibling-profile ownership of CFG blocks.
  3. A fail-closed binary publication path and tests spanning host semantics, native ABIs, large ELF placement and QEMU differential execution.
  4. An attacker-side oracle that quantifies what the current runtime format exposes without a manifest, rather than equating ciphertext entropy with resistance to devirtualization.

The implementation and its scope are described by the architecture, obfuscation, security model and analysis guide. This paper states their central contracts and the evidence supporting them.

docs.title: 2. Threat model and claims
docs.text:
The defender controls the input ELF, symbol choice, protection seeds and build process. The attacker obtains a protected ELF, can disassemble it, run or instrument it, and knows the published source code and format. An optional .myvmp.json sidecar is a diagnostic artifact and should not be distributed when its profile and CFG metadata are sensitive. We do not assume secrets can be hidden in a client-side runtime. Seeds are reproducibility and diversification inputs, not secret cryptographic keys.

The intended property is an increased cost of mapping protected machine code to the original function's semantics. We do not claim semantic indistinguishability, unbreakable obfuscation, anti-debugging, tamper resistance or a lower bound on an analyst's work. A reference oracle already recovers a useful part of the VM structure. This attacker result is part of the evaluation, not an exception hidden from it.

docs.title: 3. System architecture
docs.text:
linked ELF + selected symbol
              |
       ELF/range/relocation checks
              |
       ISA decoder and lifter  <--- AArch64 / A32 / RV64
              |
          common typed IR
              |
       CFG + liveness analysis
              |
  profile generation + block ownership
              |
   bytecode encoding + native VM runtime
              |
       ELF placement + entry detour
              |
  protected ELF + optional sidecar

The ELF frontend validates class, machine, section/segment ranges, symbol bounds and file-backed executable bytes. The ISA frontend decodes the complete selected function at its actual virtual address; it lifts registers, flags, memory, control flow, calls and the explicitly supported floating-point/vector operations into typed IR. A failure in any instruction or relocation class rejects the function. The common IR is then validated for register widths, targets and exits.

The bytecode layer identifies leaders, builds blocks and remaps control targets after expansion and physical placement. The protector can reorder non-entry blocks while retaining explicit VM branches and call continuations. The runtime is target-native assembly bundled as a checked-in byte blob generated from auditable sources. A host VM interpreter provides an independent semantic test path. Target-specific patchers decide near/far detour form and update ELF layout; AArch64 and RV64 share a parameterized ELF64 layout engine, whereas ARM32 uses its ELF32/A32 path. Publication of multi-function protection is staged so a failed selection does not leave a partially protected output.

docs.title: 3.1 Native execution boundary
docs.text: At a protected entry, the detour transfers control to the runtime, which saves the target ABI state, establishes a VM frame, locates the current physical block, selects its profile and dispatches a handler. Native call gates synchronize the register/stack state needed by unvirtualized callees, then resume VM execution. The original body is replaced by seed-derived trap fill after the entry patch. This is a native ELF rewrite: ordinary unselected code still runs as compiled.

docs.title: 3.2 Architecture support is explicit
docs.text: The shipped scalar baselines cover AArch64, ARM32 in A32 state, and RV64. AArch64 also has a tested fixed-width 128-bit Advanced SIMD subset, including vector load/store, integer/bitwise operations, selected comparisons, shifts, permutation and FP32/FP64 arithmetic with native-call ABI tests. This is not a claim of all NEON, SVE/SME, RVV, Thumb or ARM32 VFP/NEON support. Unknown or unsafe forms fail closed. The precise supported instruction boundary lives in decoder/runtime tests, not in a generic architecture label.

docs.title: 4.1 Logical ISA and profiles
docs.text: IR operations lower to a shared logical VM ISA. A VmProfile derives a physical opcode assignment from a nonzero seed; common operations may have duplicate physical encodings selected per occurrence. The profile also varies dispatcher comparison constants, native handler variants, immediate reconstruction templates, block layout and fill bytes. Thus the deployed byte sequence is not merely the source instruction sequence with permuted opcode numbers. The logical operation set and operand-size contract are, however, still common across functions. Function-specific logical semantics and independently synthesized handler families are research directions, not deployed capabilities.

docs.title: 4.2 Operand and payload encoding
docs.text: Each VM instruction declares a central operand width. Before execution, the runtime decodes an operand window using key material, current physical offset, opcode domain, owner and operand-byte index; it re-encodes the window before the next dispatch. A separate payload transform and, on AArch64, rolling block transform diversify bytes by position and block. Immediate values may be reconstructed from bounded XOR or modular shares. These layers reduce direct literal and instruction-byte exposure. They are reversible encodings: the runtime must contain the key and tables, and the published reference oracle reverses them. They should not be described as encryption against an attacker who owns the binary.

docs.title: 4.3 CFG and sibling profiles
docs.text:
The encoder gives each logical block a stable identity while allowing a different physical ordering. Sibling mode assigns blocks to one of two seeded profiles. The initial ownership algorithm uses CFG, loop, dominator and liveness information alongside seeded variation; the entry remains anchored. Each static cross-owner edge has a validated VmBridge recording source/destination profile, target/continuation, live state policy and other execution metadata. The native runtime selects the active translation/handler domain from the destination block's owner. In the current native runtime, sibling profiles share a full execution frame. A host interpreter additionally tests reversible, profile-local register/flag/vector/SP representations and live-state transfers, but target assembly does not yet execute these representation transforms.

  logical CFG:       B0 ----> B1 ----> B3
                      \      /
                       -> B2

  physical layout:   [B0:A] [B3:A] [B1:B] [B2:B]
                        |       ^       |
                        +-- bridge -----+

  A/B are profile owners, not separate operating-system processes.
  Arrows describe logical edges; byte offsets follow physical layout.

Bounded superoperators combine only eligible same-block compare/test and branch patterns. They do not cross targets, calls or memory-order boundaries. This restriction keeps behavioral equivalence testable and avoids obscuring an unsupported side effect.

docs.title: 5. Correctness and fail-closed design
docs.text: The transformation is accepted only when native decoding, IR validation, bytecode targets, VM ownership, detour reach and ELF placement satisfy their contracts. Unknown opcodes and malformed runtime metadata enter explicit failure paths. The host VM executes logical bytecode for rapid semantic tests; real protected ELFs are then run under QEMU against originals. Test layers include CLI error contracts, runtime-blob regeneration, cross-toolchain builds, multi-seed checks, native call/ABI cases, ARM32 and RV64 behavior, AArch64 SIMD differential cases and large-ELF far-detour stress. These tests are evidence for the checked cases, not a proof over all programs or compiler outputs.

docs.title: 6. Attacker-side analysis
docs.text:
An evaluator should not treat high entropy or low byte overlap as evidence that a devirtualizer cannot recover structure. We therefore maintain reference_devirtualizer.py, an oracle for the current shipped format. Given the protected ELF, architecture, runtime start and code size, it parses native runtime tables and block ranges, reverses payload/operand transforms, identifies VM instruction boundaries and logical opcodes, and reconstructs explicit branch targets plus statically inferable fallthrough edges. It does not require the sidecar. With one, it compares recovered boundaries, owners and CFG edges to ground truth. Its regression suite includes AArch64 single and sibling modes, ARM32 and RV64, plus malformed size, target and owner checks.

For AArch64 single-VM mode, mapping a physical opcode to a logical one additionally uses patched native dispatcher comparisons and the comparison order in this open-source repository. Sibling AArch64 and ARM32/RV64 use exposed runtime translation tables. The oracle does not model handler effects, dynamic VM-return edges, or lift bytecode back to source-level semantic IR. A logical VM opcode count is therefore not an IR recovery count. This distinction defines a concrete next benchmark: recover handler semantics and compare normalized IR/CFG across profiles and compiler versions.

docs.title: 7. Evaluation and interpretation
docs.text:
The checked-in benchmark snapshot was captured on Ubuntu 22.04 with GCC cross-toolchains and QEMU 6.2. Each listed protected ELF had stdout compared byte-for-byte with its original. The byte-quality sample compares a selected native function range to concatenated encrypted VM block ranges, not entire files.

Fixture Native bytes VM payload bytes Payload entropy (bits/byte) Identical QEMU stdout ARM32/A32 VM probe 68 264 7.241544 yes AArch64 branch operations 76 197 7.081294 yes RV64 loop 32 141 6.627036 yes

For these three fixtures, same-position and tested literal/word exposure ratios were zero. These are small examples and do not establish resistance to semantic recovery. The ELF packaging cost also varies: in the snapshot, the AArch64 one-function case grew by 65,536 bytes; RV64 grew by 7,857 bytes for one selected function and 16,375 bytes for three; the ARM32 example reused existing space and showed no file-size growth. A 135,275,392-byte AArch64 PIE far-detour case also grew by 65,536 bytes and preserved observed QEMU stdout. Runtime slowdowns are not reported in this snapshot; no general performance claim follows from it.

The attacker oracle gives a contrasting observation. For its sibling-mode integration fixtures (seeds 12345/67890), it recovered 27 VM instructions and all 6 sidecar CFG edges on AArch64, 37 instructions and 6/6 edges on ARM32, and 29 instructions and 2/2 edges on RV64. These exact matches show that diversification and reversible encoding did not conceal that structure in these cases. The fixtures are too small to establish cross-sample attack cost or a statistical security result.

docs.title: 8. Limitations, validity and research agenda
docs.text:
The current native system has two sibling profiles rather than N-way heterogeneous VM models. Profiles vary encoding and handlers but share the logical ISA and native VM frame. Host-only state-representation experiments and a bounded sequence miner must not be confused with generated native state bridges or synthesized operators. AArch64 SIMD is a defined subset, and ARM32/RV64 vector extensions are not implied. Shared objects, TLS, unwinding, unusual relocations, new compiler idioms and very large production binaries need broader qualification. Selected symbols must be known and safely patchable.

Internal validity depends on the fixtures, compiler flags and QEMU behavior checks. External validity is limited by the absence of large independent application corpora, human reverse-engineering studies, and measured devirtualizer time/cost. Our reference oracle is format-aware and open-source, so its success does not quantify how fast an analyst with no source could reproduce it. Conversely, its failure to lift semantic IR does not prove that such lifting is hard. Future experiments should report recovered source-level IR/CFG, trace-shape alignment, handler clustering, tool runtime and human effort alongside size and protected-program overhead.

docs.title: 9. Related work and ethics
docs.text:
Virtualization and attacker normalization are discussed in the SoK on automatic deobfuscation. Tigress's virtualization documentation describes design options such as duplicate instructions and superoperators. These are conceptual references, not a claim that CactiVM reproduces either implementation. Binary rewriting and platform correctness are informed by E9Patch, the Arm ELF ABI and the RISC-V ELF psABI. The full design bibliography is in research notes.

Software protection is dual-use: the same transformations can conceal malicious logic. This project publishes format details, limitations and an attacker-side oracle to make security claims falsifiable. Users remain responsible for applying it only to software they are authorized to modify and for preserving legal and operational auditability.

docs.title: 10. Reproducibility
docs.text: The repository is GPL-3.0-only. Start with build instructions, then run make release-check, make reference-devirtualizer-test and the relevant architecture/QEMU targets in testing. The exact benchmark environment, inputs, selections and values are in the checked-in JSON evidence. protect sidecars preserve seeds, profile and block metadata for controlled reproduction; they should be handled as diagnostic artifacts. A complete experiment should archive input/output hashes, toolchain and QEMU versions, selected symbols, flags, seeds, sidecars, observed behavior and machine-readable analysis reports.

docs.title: 11. Conclusion
docs.text: CactiVM demonstrates a modular, selective binary virtualization pipeline across three ELF architectures, with explicit correctness gates and real-runtime execution tests. Its layered profiles and sibling ownership change the protected execution surface, but the present runtime format leaves VM instructions and static CFG recoverable. The result supports a narrower and more useful conclusion than “strong obfuscation”: the system is deployable for qualified selected functions, while meaningful claims about analysis resistance require semantic attacker baselines, larger corpora and measured costs.

docs.title: Published benchmark snapshot
docs.text:
中文 · Machine-readable JSON

This is the evidence behind the compact tables in the README. It is a checked-in snapshot from 2026-09-04, generated with the repository fixtures and the normal myvmp CLI on Ubuntu 22.04. Every protected output listed here was executed under QEMU and its stdout compared byte-for-byte with the original.

docs.title: What was measured
docs.text:
The quality comparison uses the original native function range as its input and the concatenated, encrypted VM block payload ranges recorded by the output manifest as its protected sample. This answers whether recognizable native bytes and aligned words leak into the encrypted bytecode. It deliberately does not compare entire ELF files: headers, libraries and all unselected functions are expected to stay unchanged.

The separate ELF-size cases show packaging cost. They include ARM32, AArch64 and RV64; one-function and three-function selection; and a 135,275,392-byte AArch64 PIE that forces the range-safe far-page detour. Exact values and environment versions are in the JSON.

docs.title: Interpreting the result
docs.text:
Zero positional and literal exposure, higher entropy and a passing regression threshold are useful evidence that the codec/encryption pipeline is operating. They are not a cryptographic proof and do not imply that virtualization cannot be analyzed. See the security model before making deployment decisions.

To produce a report for your own binary, use generate_analysis_report.py. Results depend on toolchain, input, selected symbols, seeds and VM mode; published numbers are examples, not promises for every ELF.

docs.title: Research Notes and References
docs.text:
中文

This is a design bibliography, not a claim that myVMP copies any product or source. The project implements its own C++ architecture, IR, bytecode, runtimes and ELF transformation. References were used to understand established designs, attacker workflows, ABI rules and measurement pitfalls. License terms of referenced code must be reviewed independently; no external source should be copied without compatible licensing and provenance.

docs.title: Virtualization protection and devirtualization
docs.text:
• SoK: Automatic Deobfuscation of Virtualization-protected Applications — attacker models for recovering fetch/decode/dispatch/handler structure and normalizing VM traces; motivated per-block/profile diversity and honest limits on multi-VM complexity. Paper
  • Matryoshka / process-level nested virtualization — evidence that nesting can raise analysis cost while imposing substantial overhead; motivated sibling VMs before unrestricted recursive nesting. Slides
  • Tigress Virtualize — duplicate instructions, operand-location variation, superoperators, dispatch diversity and reentrant interpreters; informed bounded, testable polymorphism rather than a single opcode permutation. Documentation
  • Recent obfuscation/devirtualization literature reviewed during quality planning — used as prompts for attacker-oriented measurement and evolving VM signatures, not as implementation specifications. arXiv:2601.10261, arXiv:2603.18355, SSRN 5147457, IEEE Access reference

docs.title: Open-source virtualization and binary protection
docs.text:
• VMPacker — ARM64 Linux ELF function virtualization, custom bytecode, opcode randomization, encrypted/reordered bytecode and injection workflow. It reinforced the value of a binary-level frontend and strict module separation. Repository
  • xVMP — LLVM-level virtualization with per-basic-block ideas; informed block identity, block-local crypto domains and quality comparisons while myVMP remains binary-level. Repository
  • binprotect — x64 PE binary virtualization and per-handler layout diversity; useful attacker/implementation reference but not a reusable ARM ELF design. Repository
  • Kiteshield — x86-64 ELF packing and function encryption; informed separation between packing/encryption and semantic VM virtualization. Repository
  • covirt — VM/MBA/self-modifying experiments and documented VM-call failure modes; reinforced the need for an explicit, validated bridge ABI. Repository
  • Miasm — mature lifting and analysis concepts; useful as a future differential oracle, while myVMP retains a compact project-owned IR and no Python runtime dependency. Repository

Community analyses of commercial protectors, including VMProtect-protected samples, were used to study recognizable dispatcher loops, handler normalization, rolling decode state, operand recovery and trace-based attacks. These analyses motivated changing representation at build, block, instruction and handler levels. myVMP does not claim compatibility with, or reproduction of, VMProtect internals.

docs.title: Binary rewriting
docs.text:
• E9Patch — practical static binary rewriting and placement constraints. Repository, paper
  • LIEF — ELF object model and binary transformation API; useful comparison for segment, section and dynamic-table repair. Repository, ELF API
  • Binary rewriting research on safe patch placement and layout informed fail-closed planning and real-ELF stress tests. DOI 10.1145/3546568, STTT article

docs.title: Architecture and ABI standards
docs.text:
• Arm AArch64 ELF ABI
  • RISC-V unprivileged ISA
  • RISC-V compressed extension
  • RISC-V ELF psABI
  • x86-64 psABI and Intel SDM are preparatory references for a future x86-64 backend.

Standards, rather than protector writeups, are authoritative for instruction semantics, relocations, calling conventions and ELF behavior.

docs.title: Android native platform research
docs.text: The long-term Android assessment uses official Android NDK ABI, JNI, native-build, 16 KiB page-size, packaging and signing documentation plus AOSP Bionic linker notes. It concludes that current AArch64 ELF machinery is a strong starting point, but Android support requires a pre-sign NDK .so pipeline and platform-specific compatibility gates. See Android native protection vision for the analysis and sources.

docs.title: Testing methodology
docs.text:
• Csmith informed the optional randomized compiler-output stress layer. Deterministic checked-in fixtures remain primary because failures must be reproducible and minimized.
  • Attacker-oriented review asks whether an analyst can identify a global opcode map, plaintext operand stream, stable block order, uniform handler template or bridge ABI. Each question maps to a measurable diversity or correctness gate.

docs.title: Ideas adopted
docs.text:
1. Function-level binary virtualization with a project-owned IR.
  2. Per-build and per-occurrence physical opcode diversity.
  3. Unified rolling operand encoding across the logical opcode set.
  4. CFG-aware blocks, encrypted key evolution and movable physical layout.
  5. Bounded superoperators and native handler variants.
  6. Explicit sibling-VM ownership and bridge contracts instead of ad-hoc recursion.
  7. Transactional ELF publication and fail-closed validation.
  8. Reproducible manifests plus behavior, diversity, exposure and cost measurement.

docs.title: Ideas deliberately deferred or rejected
docs.text:
• treating high entropy as proof of protection;
  • silently passing unknown native instructions through the VM;
  • unrestricted mutually recursive interpreters without a state/exception ABI;
  • whole-program virtualization as the default deployment model;
  • copying proprietary formats or incompatible open-source implementations.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
中文

The AArch64, ARM32/A32 and RV64 scalar function-protection baselines, dynamic operand codec, CFG-aware bytecode, sibling multi-VM, real-ELF behavior suites and large-placement stress tests are implemented. The next priorities are intentionally concise.

docs.title: Release readiness
docs.text:
• publish GPL-3.0-only versioned releases using the documented signed-tag/checksum policy;
  • add reproducible-build evidence and CI across supported toolchains;
  • stabilize machine-readable CLI schemas and diagnostic error categories;
  • add packaged-tool smoke tests and compatibility fixtures for multiple compiler versions.
  • consider native Windows/macOS host ports only when demand justifies maintaining ELF and target-tool compatibility layers; WSL2/container workflows are the supported baseline.

docs.title: Correctness and platform breadth
docs.text:
• broaden the implemented AArch64 fixed-width Advanced SIMD subset only when new forms have decoder, typed-lane, native runtime and QEMU ABI coverage; keep SVE/SME and RVV separate future designs;
  • extend remaining uncommon atomics, relocations and compiler-specific scalar forms;
  • strengthen shared-object, TLS, exception/unwind and very-large-application qualification;
  • broaden ARM32 compiler-corpus qualification while keeping Thumb/VFP/NEON explicit opt-in work.

docs.title: Quality and analysis resistance
docs.text:
• initial CFG dominator, natural-loop and multi-class liveness analysis now drives seeded sibling ownership and live-state bridge metadata; the host sibling interpreter now executes deterministic reversible register/flag/vector/SP representation transforms at live-state boundaries, but native runtime bridge integration remains future work;
  • scripts/reference_devirtualizer.py now reverses runtime bytecode whitening and operand encoding on AArch64, ARM32 and RV64 without a sidecar, recovering VM instructions and static CFG edges; optional sidecars quantify exact matches. Next recover handler effects and source-level semantic IR, including dynamic call/return edges, and measure the cost across compilers/functions rather than treating byte entropy as protection evidence;
  • integrate the experimental FunctionVmIsa descriptor into a real per-function encoder and runtime grammar before claiming function-specific bytecode formats;
  • a bounded, same-basic-block miner now reports frequent side-effect-free scalar sequences; synthesize profile-specific bytecode superoperators only with generated handlers and differential semantic validation;
  • add more independently structured dispatch/handler families with measured signature reduction;
  • experiment with selective nested protection only if it materially improves attacker workload beyond sibling mode at acceptable cost;
  • improve automated report comparison across releases, compilers and seeds.

docs.title: New architectures
docs.text:
• design an x86-64 frontend/runtime using the common IR, profile, codec, manifest and ELF64 writer contracts;
  • keep ISA semantics and detours target-specific rather than contaminating common bytecode;
  • consider other executable formats only after ELF architecture boundaries remain clean.

docs.title: Long-term Android native target
docs.text:
• treat Android as an NDK .so protection and build-integration project, not as a claim of Java/Kotlin/Dex or whole-APK obfuscation;
  • begin, if approved, with an arm64-v8a compatibility/liftability corpus before writing Android artifacts;
  • require Android ET_DYN relocation/RELRO, 4/16 KiB alignment, JNI, Gradle, APK/AAB and signing-order gates before declaring support;
  • see the research-only Android native protection vision.

Roadmap items are not support promises. A feature becomes supported only after host semantics, target-runtime behavior, malformed-input handling and release documentation all pass together.

docs.title: Security Model and Limitations
docs.text: 中文

docs.title: Intended threat model
docs.text: myVMP raises the cost of static inspection and routine patching of selected user-mode functions in Linux ELF binaries. It assumes an analyst can possess and execute the protected file, inspect memory, trace instructions and compare samples. The objective is diversity and analysis friction, not secrecy against an all-powerful local adversary.

docs.title: What the design provides
docs.text:
• selected native semantics are replaced by encrypted, encoded VM instructions;
  • source/VM correspondence changes across seeds and physical blocks;
  • original native body bytes are destroyed after a validated detour is installed;
  • sibling mode changes VM ownership dynamically across CFG edges;
  • manifests and deterministic seeds support auditing and reproducible diagnosis;
  • malformed/unsupported inputs fail before final publication;
  • QEMU and host regressions continuously check semantic preservation.

docs.title: What it does not provide
docs.text:
• a proof against devirtualization, symbolic execution or dynamic tracing;
  • anti-debugging, anti-dump, remote attestation or a secure key store;
  • confidentiality once plaintext state/semantics are observed during execution;
  • automatic protection of every compiler output, kernel code or privileged instructions;
  • memory-safety hardening of the protected application itself;
  • tamper-proof manifests or signed releases.

An analyst can eventually model fetch/decode/dispatch/handler behavior. Multi-VM and polymorphism make normalization more expensive, but complexity is not equivalent to a cryptographic guarantee.

The current AArch64, ARM32 and RV64 runtime formats expose physical VM block boundaries, owner indices, VM instruction fields and static CFG edges to analysis even when no sidecar is published. The owner-table and bytecode transforms use keys stored in the runtime header; they are reversible encodings, not confidentiality boundaries. This does not by itself recover handler effects, dynamic return edges or source-level semantics. The reference runtime oracle measures this exposure.

docs.title: Fail-closed boundaries
docs.text:
Protection is rejected for unsupported machines/classes, missing or zero-sized symbols, unknown instructions, unsafe relocation ranges, unrepresentable branches, invalid CFG or VM metadata, payload/runtime limits and inconsistent sibling partitions. ARM32/A32 rejects Thumb, VFP/NEON and privileged families; sibling multi-VM is supported. x86-64 target protection is not implemented.

The exact instruction boundary is defined by decoder/lifter code and release fixtures. AArch64 includes the documented, regression-tested fixed 128-bit Advanced SIMD subset; other NEON forms, SVE/SVE2/SME, RV64 Vector and platform-specific families must not be assumed supported merely because a runtime preserves vector register state.

docs.title: Operational recommendations
docs.text:
• Protect narrowly chosen high-value functions, not an entire very large application.
  • Keep unsupported/environmental operations in small native helpers reached through tested call gates.
  • Use multiple representative seeds during qualification and one controlled seed per release build.
  • Compare complete behavior under realistic inputs, concurrency and error paths.
  • Treat sidecars as sensitive diagnostic metadata when they expose build profiles.
  • Sign final artifacts using an external release system and retain unprotected symbols only as long as needed for protection/debugging.
  • Measure runtime and size on production-like hardware; QEMU ratios are regression data, not capacity planning.

docs.title: Reporting issues
docs.text: A useful defect report contains target architecture, compiler/linker versions, minimal source or redistributable ELF, symbol name, exact command and seed, dry-run logs, sidecar, original/protected outputs and the smallest behavior mismatch. Do not publish proprietary binaries or secret production seeds.

docs.title: Documentation Website Publishing
docs.text:
中文

The repository keeps documentation source as Markdown under docs/. The GitHub Actions workflow in .github/workflows/docs.yml installs pinned MkDocs and Material for MkDocs versions, performs a strict build, verifies Mermaid containers with a Python standard-library checker, and publishes the generated site to the separate gh-pages branch. The check does not assume that rg is installed on the runner. Generated HTML is not maintained or committed on the source branch.

docs.title: One-time GitHub setup
docs.text:
1. In repository Settings → Actions → General, allow the workflow to have read and write repository contents (or otherwise grant GITHUB_TOKEN the contents: write permission).
  2. Push this workflow and the MkDocs configuration to master (or main). The first run creates/updates gh-pages.
  3. In Settings → Pages, select Deploy from a branch, choose gh-pages, and select /(root).
  4. Later commits affecting docs/** or mkdocs.yml publish automatically. A manual run is also available from Actions → Publish documentation → Run workflow; select master or main as the source branch for that run.

The site is built in GitHub Actions only. Do not add the generated site/ directory to the source branch; it is a transient build product. The deployment workflow force-updates the generated contents of gh-pages, so hand-edits on that branch will be replaced.

If Actions reports exit code 127, expand the failing step: it means a shell command was not found. The former Mermaid check called rg without installing it; the current check uses python scripts/check_mermaid_site.py site, and both MkDocs invocations use python -m mkdocs. A local, unpushed workflow edit cannot affect a GitHub run: push the source branch, confirm the new commit SHA in the run, then inspect the generated Pages site.

docs.title: Testing and Release Validation
docs.text: 中文

docs.title: Test layers
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    U[Host unit semantics] --> L[Decoder/lifter fixtures]
    L --> E[ELF planning and writing]
    E --> Q[QEMU original/protected behavior]
    Q --> D[Multi-seed diversity and cost]
    D --> S[Large ELF and malformed-input stress]
    S --> R[Release package smoke test]

Host tests prove IR, bytecode, codecs, profile validation, VM execution and branch encoders. Target tests compile real functions, protect them and compare complete program behavior under QEMU. Quality tests then ensure equivalent outputs are not accidentally identical across seeds.

docs.title: Core commands
docs.text:
make test
make integration-test
make generated-fixture-test

The GitHub Actions workflow now only builds and publishes the documentation site; it does not compile the project or run tests. Run the commands below in a local release environment or a dedicated hardware test job. Cross-compilation, QEMU, seed-sweep, large-ELF and generated-runtime gates are deliberately kept out of routine documentation publishing.

docs.title: AArch64 release gates
docs.text:
make arm64-integration-test
make arm64-micro-lift-test
make arm64-liftability-report
make arm64-protect-dry-run-test
make arm64-elf-patch-test
make arm64-vm-protect-test
make arm64-simd-test
make arm64-far-elf-test
make bytecode-seed-sweep
make multi-vm-quality-test
make check-aarch64-runtime

The VM behavior suite covers scalar integer/flags/control flow, memory widths and modes, direct/indirect/tail/internal calls, GOT/global addressing, scalar FP32/FP64 and conditional FP, exclusive/acquire/release atomics and supported Armv8.1 compare/exchange. Sibling tests exercise branch, call and memory CFGs.

arm64-simd-test protects a real Advanced SIMD function in single and sibling modes and compares QEMU output. It covers integer lanes, bitwise/compare/select, shifts, EXT, Q memory, FP32/FP64 vector arithmetic, zeroing and q0-q7 native-call synchronization. It also verifies that the two sibling profiles assign different physical values to all nine vector opcode families.

arm64-far-elf-test builds a real PIE with more than 129 MiB of executable file-backed padding. It forces the payload beyond direct-branch range, verifies the ADRP/ADD/BR detour and compares behavior under QEMU.

docs.title: RV64 release gates
docs.text:
make riscv64-fixture-test
make riscv64-liftability-report
make riscv64-vm-protect-test
make riscv64-elf-stress-test
make riscv64-multi-vm-quality-test
make check-riscv64-runtime

The stress suite covers static/non-PIE, PIE, lazy/immediate binding, shared objects, global/GOT access, calls, TLS/RELRO-sensitive layouts, batch protection, large placement, loops, switches and mixed-width RVC/native instruction streams used by the corpus.

docs.title: ARM32/A32 release gates
docs.text:
make arm32-elf-parser-test
make arm32-vm-protect-test
make check-arm32-runtime

The QEMU gate executes the same real ELF before and after protection with two independent single-VM seeds and sibling multi-VM. Its A32 corpus covers integer/logical operations, shifted operands, flags and predicates, memory, multiplication, CFG blocks and return.

docs.title: Quality acceptance
docs.text: Seed sweeps require unique payloads and manifests. Sibling suites require behavior equality, actual bridges, meaningful ownership balance, high pairwise ciphertext distance and bounded output/runtime ratios. Numeric thresholds live in the scripts so changes are reviewed with the measurement logic.

docs.title: Pre-release checklist
docs.text:
1. Start from a clean build directory and run make -j$(nproc) test.
  2. Run make docs-check to validate local links and bilingual document parity.
  3. Verify all checked-in runtime blobs.
  4. Run the complete AArch64, ARM32 and RV64 gates available in the release environment.
  5. Run ASan/UBSan and git diff --check.
  6. Build make package, unpack it in a temporary directory and run myvmp --help.
  7. Protect and execute one AArch64, ARM32 and RV64 smoke fixture using the packaged tool.
  8. Confirm English/Chinese docs and all relative links are included.
  9. Record compiler, cross-toolchain, QEMU and host versions with release artifacts.

Missing optional tools may cause individual scripts to skip. A public release should use an environment where primary architecture gates execute rather than skip.
